title: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
summary: How networks find body keypoints with heatmaps and sub-pixel decoding, how top-down and bottom-up (part affinity field) systems differ, how COCO scores poses with OKS, and how apps turn keypoints into angles.
outcomes: Decode a keypoint heatmap with argmax and the quarter-pixel shift, and explain the resolution limit
Explain when top-down beats bottom-up and how part affinity fields group keypoints into people
Compute Object Keypoint Similarity for a predicted pose with per-keypoint sigmas and object area
Compute a joint angle from three keypoints and explain why 2D angles mislead under foreshortening
Describe how BlazePose stays real time and what 3D lifting from 2D keypoints does

lessons.title: What a pose model outputs and the top-down pipeline

blocks.md:
In the detection course a model drew a box around each person and NMS removed the duplicates. A box says *where* a person is, but not whether their arm is raised or their knee is bent. **Pose estimation** answers that: for each person it predicts a fixed list of **keypoints** (also called landmarks or joints), such as nose, shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees and ankles, each with an (x, y) position and a score.

A skeleton of 17 points is a much smaller, more structured signal than the pixels. Fitness apps count squats from it, sign language and gesture systems read it, and you can write plain rules against it ("is the knee angle below 100 degrees?").

The **COCO keypoints** benchmark labels each person with 17 keypoints: nose, two eyes, two ears, two shoulders, two elbows, two wrists, two hips, two knees and two ankles. A label is a flat list `[x1, y1, v1, ..., x17, y17, v17]` where the **visibility flag** `v` is 0 for not labeled, 1 for labeled but not visible (occluded), and 2 for labeled and visible.

Other systems use other skeletons. MediaPipe Pose Landmarker (based on BlazePose) returns 33 landmarks, adding points such as heels, foot tips and three points per hand (pinky, index and thumb), plus a `visibility` likelihood per landmark.

Why not just add 34 numbers to the end of a CNN and regress the coordinates directly? That works, but it is hard to train well: the network must turn spatial features into absolute numbers through fully connected layers, and a regression trained with a squared loss tends toward the *mean* plausible location when a joint is ambiguous. The BlazePose paper makes this point: regression approaches are cheaper but predict mean coordinate values and struggle with ambiguous poses.

Stacked Hourglass, Simple Baselines and HRNet all predict a **heatmap** per keypoint instead, an image whose bright spot marks the joint. The next lesson opens up the heatmap.

blocks.title: Top-down pose estimation, one person at a time

scenes.caption: Stage 1 is the detector from the previous course. It finds every person and returns one box per person after NMS.
Each box is extended to a fixed 4:3 height-to-width ratio, cropped and resized to 256x192 (as in HRNet), so every person reaches the keypoint network at the same scale.
The keypoint network outputs one heatmap per keypoint, smaller than the crop: in Simple Baselines a 256x192 crop gives 64x48 heatmaps.
Decoding finds the peak of each heatmap and maps it back through the crop to image coordinates. The peak height doubles as a per-keypoint score.
The network runs once per detected person. Five people means five crops and five forward passes, so cost grows with the crowd. Lesson 3 returns to this.

blocks.md: This two-stage design is called **top-down**: detect people first, then estimate one pose per box. Simple Baselines (Xiao et al., 2018) and HRNet (Sun et al., 2019) are both top-down; at test time they reuse a Faster R-CNN person detector and run the keypoint network on each box. The alternative, **bottom-up**, finds all keypoints in the whole image first and then groups them into people. Lesson 3 compares the two.

A top-down pose model inherits every mistake of its detector. If two people overlap and NMS merges their boxes, or the detector misses someone, the keypoint network has no way to recover that person. OpenPose's authors call this **early commitment**.
A pose model's output is a fixed, ordered list of keypoints per person, each with a position and a confidence. Everything downstream (metrics, angles, rep counting) is arithmetic on that list.

blocks.question: A COCO ground-truth person has the left wrist marked with v = 1. What does that mean?
options: The annotator placed the wrist, but it is hidden (for example behind the torso)
The wrist was not annotated at all, so it is ignored
The wrist is visible and annotated
The wrist was predicted by a model, not a person
blocks.explain: v = 0 means not labeled, v = 1 labeled but not visible, v = 2 labeled and visible. Occluded joints still get a position, so a model is expected to guess where a hidden wrist is.

blocks.question: A gym camera sees a tight group of three people, and the person detector returns only two boxes because NMS suppressed one overlapping box. What does a top-down pose system output?
options: Three skeletons, because the keypoint network sees all joints in the crop
Two skeletons; the suppressed person gets no pose at all
Three skeletons, but the third has low scores
Zero skeletons, because the boxes overlap
blocks.explain: The keypoint network only runs on boxes the detector returned. A person lost at the detection stage is lost for good: this is the early commitment problem of top-down methods.

lessons.title: Heatmaps: training targets, argmax and sub-pixel decoding

blocks.md: A **keypoint heatmap** is a small grayscale image, one per keypoint type, where each cell holds a score for "the joint is here". The network is trained to output, for keypoint $k$, a 2D Gaussian blob centered on the true location $(x_k, y_k)$. Stacked Hourglass (Newell et al., 2016), Simple Baselines and HRNet all train this target with a mean squared error (MSE) loss between predicted and target heatmaps; the Hourglass and HRNet papers state a standard deviation of 1 heatmap pixel.

blocks.tex: H_k(x, y) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x - x_k)^2 + (y - y_k)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), \quad \mathcal{L} = \sum_{k}\sum_{(x,y)} \big(\hat H_k(x,y) - H_k(x,y)\big)^2
blocks.caption: Target heatmap with sigma = 1 heatmap pixel, and the MSE loss summed over keypoints and cells (papers differ in how they normalize the sum).

blocks.md:
Why does this train better than regressing numbers? The output keeps the spatial layout of the image, so the convolutional layers only need to say "this location looks like a left knee", which they are good at. It also lets the network express doubt: an occluded wrist can produce two weaker blobs instead of a single averaged point halfway between them.

The cost is resolution. Heatmaps are smaller than the input: Stacked Hourglass maps a 256x256 input to 64x64 heatmaps, and Simple Baselines turns a 256x192 crop into 64x48 heatmaps. One heatmap cell covers 4x4 input pixels.

blocks.title: Decoding one 7x7 heatmap for a knee

scenes.caption: Toy 7x7 heatmap (a real one is 64x48). The true knee is at x = 3.35, y = 2.7, between cells. Simplified: we pretend the network output the exact Gaussian target.
Argmax: the largest cell is 0.90 at column 3, row 3. Taking it as the answer gives (3, 3), off by 0.46 cells from the truth.
Horizontal step: right neighbor 0.77 beats left neighbor 0.38, so x moves a quarter cell right, from 3 to 3.25.
Vertical step: the cell above (0.74) beats the cell below (0.40), so y moves a quarter cell up, from 3 to 2.75. Result (3.25, 2.75), now 0.11 cells from the truth.
Mapped back to the crop at 4 pixels per cell: argmax alone was 1.84 px off, the refined estimate is 0.45 px off. That gap matters for strict metrics.

blocks.md: The quarter-pixel shift is not a trick invented for this course. Newell et al. write that "the prediction is offset by a quarter of a pixel in the direction of its next highest neighbor" to improve accuracy at high precision thresholds, and the Simple Baselines code does exactly this per axis, comparing the left and right neighbors for x and the upper and lower neighbors for y.

blocks.title: The decode step, as in the Simple Baselines code
blocks.code:
def decode(hm, stride=4):
    r, c = argmax_2d(hm)              # row, col of peak
    x, y = float(c), float(r)
    H, W = len(hm), len(hm[0])
    if 1 < c < W - 1 and 1 < r < H - 1:   # skip borders
        x += 0.25 * sign(hm[r][c + 1] - hm[r][c - 1])
        y += 0.25 * sign(hm[r + 1][c] - hm[r - 1][c])
    score = hm[r][c]
    return x * stride, y * stride, score

scenes.caption: Find the peak cell of the 7x7 heatmap.
Start from the integer cell coordinates.
Right (0.77) minus left (0.38) is positive, so x gains 0.25.
Below (0.40) minus above (0.74) is negative, so y loses 0.25.
The peak value is the keypoint score. Scale by the stride to get crop pixels; a later affine step maps crop pixels to the original image.

blocks.prompt: With argmax alone and no refinement, what is the worst-case error per axis, in heatmap cells and in input pixels for a 256x192 crop with 64x48 heatmaps?
blocks.reveal: Half a cell per axis, because the truth can sit anywhere up to the cell boundary. At 4 input pixels per cell that is 2 pixels per axis, or about 2.8 pixels diagonally. On a small person in the original image that error is scaled up further when the crop is mapped back, which is why heatmap resolution and sub-pixel decoding both show up in ablations.

blocks.md:
Two other standard test-time steps: run the crop and its horizontal mirror through the network and average the heatmaps (after flipping back and swapping left and right channels). Newell et al. report this gives about 1% on validation, and Simple Baselines and HRNet use it too.

Resolution is also why architecture matters. In the Simple Baselines ablation on COCO val2017, 32x24 heatmaps instead of 64x48 cost its ResNet-50 model 2.5 AP (70.4 to 67.9), and halving the input to 128x96 drops it to 60.6 AP.

The network never outputs coordinates. It outputs heatmaps, and a small hand-written decoder (argmax, quarter-cell shift, scale by stride, undo the crop) turns them into numbers. Bugs in that decoder, such as swapping x and y or forgetting the crop offset, look like a bad model.

blocks.question: At the argmax cell, the left neighbor is 0.55 and the right neighbor is 0.52; the cells above and below are both 0.30. Using the quarter-offset rule, where does the keypoint go relative to the argmax cell (col, row)?
options: (col + 0.25, row)
(col, row)
(col - 0.25, row)
blocks.explain: The left neighbor is higher, so x shifts a quarter cell left. The vertical neighbors are equal, so sign(0) = 0 and y does not move.

blocks.question: A team swaps a 64x48 heatmap head for a 16x12 one to save compute, keeping the same decoder. What do you expect on COCO AP?
options: No change, because the quarter offset fixes quantization
An increase, because coarser maps are smoother
A drop, mostly at strict thresholds, because each cell now covers 16x16 input pixels
A drop only for keypoints that are occluded
blocks.explain: Quantization error grows with cell size, and a quarter-cell shift only removes part of it. Strict OKS thresholds such as 0.75 punish a few pixels of error, so they suffer first.

lessons.title: Backbones, top-down versus bottom-up, and part affinity fields

blocks.md:
Every heatmap network faces the same tension: recognizing *which* joint needs a large receptive field and deep, low-resolution features, but *placing* it needs high resolution. Three designs from the primary papers handle this differently.

- **Stacked Hourglass** (Newell et al., 2016): repeated down-then-up modules ("hourglasses") with skip connections. Eight hourglasses are stacked, each producing heatmaps that receive the loss (intermediate supervision).
- **Simple Baselines** (Xiao et al., 2018): a ResNet followed by three transposed convolution (deconvolution) layers, each with 256 filters, 4x4 kernels and stride 2, then a 1x1 convolution to K heatmaps.
- **HRNet** (Sun et al., 2019): keeps a high-resolution branch through the whole network and adds lower-resolution branches in parallel, repeatedly fusing information across them, instead of recovering resolution at the end.

blocks.title: COCO test-dev keypoint AP, as reported in the HRNet paper

scenes.caption: Two bottom-up methods from the HRNet comparison table. Neither needs a person detector.
Top-down methods at 384x288 input, all using a person detector. The table's best bottom-up entry, MultiPoseNet at 69.6, trails them by 4 to 6 AP.

blocks.md: If top-down is more accurate, why does bottom-up exist? Two reasons. A top-down system runs the keypoint network once per person, so its cost grows with the crowd, and it fails when the detector fails. A **bottom-up** system runs one network on the whole image to find *all* keypoints of *all* people, then groups them. The OpenPose authors argue this decouples runtime from the number of people.

scenes.caption: Illustrative costs, not measurements. With these numbers top-down is cheaper for one to four people and bottom-up wins from five on. Move the sliders: the crossover is where det + p x N equals b + g x N.
A faster per-person network (4 ms) pushes the crossover out past 13 people, which is why top-down stays popular when frames hold only a few people.

blocks.md:
Bottom-up needs a way to decide which detected left elbow belongs with which left wrist. OpenPose (Cao et al., 2017) predicts, alongside the keypoint heatmaps, a **part affinity field (PAF)** for each limb: a 2-channel map that stores, at every pixel lying on that limb, the unit vector pointing from one joint to the other (for example elbow to wrist), and zero elsewhere.

To score a candidate pair of detections $d_{j1}$ (elbow) and $d_{j2}$ (wrist), sample the PAF along the straight segment between them and measure how well it points in the segment's direction:

blocks.tex: E = \int_{0}^{1} L_c\big(p(u)\big) \cdot \frac{d_{j2} - d_{j1}}{\lVert d_{j2} - d_{j1} \rVert_2}\, du, \qquad p(u) = (1-u)\, d_{j1} + u\, d_{j2}
blocks.caption: OpenPose line integral over the limb field L_c. In practice it is approximated by summing the field at evenly spaced samples along the segment.

blocks.title: PAF scores for 3 elbows and 3 wrists

scenes.caption: Three people, so three elbow and three wrist candidates. Each cell is the mean of the field-dot-direction at 10 samples along the segment. Simplified PAF: unit vectors within 3 px of each true forearm.
Nearest-neighbor grouping goes wrong: E2 is 15.8 px from W1 but 30.0 px from its own wrist W2. Greedy by distance pairs E2-W1, E3-W3, then E1-W2.
E2-W1 still scores 0.58 because the first part of that segment runs through E2's real forearm field. Partial overlap gives partial credit.
Maximum-weight bipartite matching picks one wrist per elbow to maximize the total score: E1-W1, E2-W2, E3-W3 with total 3.0, the correct people.

blocks.md: Matching a full body this way is a hard multi-way graph problem. OpenPose relaxes it in two steps: use only the edges of a spanning tree skeleton (neck to shoulder, shoulder to elbow, and so on), and solve each limb type as an independent bipartite matching, which the Hungarian algorithm solves optimally. Shared joints then chain the limbs into full people. The heavy work is one CNN pass; the matching is cheap.

Bottom-up is not free of crowd effects. The CNN pass is constant, but the number of candidate pairs per limb grows with the number of people, and the whole image goes through the network at one input size, so small, distant people cover only a few heatmap pixels, while top-down resizes every person to the same crop size.

blocks.question: Which change would most directly break the PAF score for a correct elbow-wrist pair?
options: Another person stands far away in the frame
The predicted field along the segment points sideways, across the forearm, instead of along it
The elbow heatmap peak is 0.6 instead of 0.9
The PAF predicts the wrist-to-elbow direction, and scoring uses the same convention
blocks.explain: The score is the dot product between the field and the segment direction. If the field along the segment points sideways, the dot products shrink. Distant people do not touch this segment, the peak height does not enter E, and a consistent direction convention is fine.

blocks.question: A drone films a stadium crowd of 200 people from far away, and you need rough poses on a fixed compute budget. Which design fits better?
options: Top-down, because it is more accurate on COCO
Top-down with a larger crop size
Either; the cost is identical
Bottom-up, because one network pass covers everyone and cost barely grows with 200 people
blocks.explain: Top-down would run the keypoint network 200 times per frame. Bottom-up runs once and groups with cheap matching. Accuracy per person may be lower, but the cost model favors bottom-up at this crowd size.

lessons.title: Scoring poses with Object Keypoint Similarity

blocks.md:
Detection is scored by matching predicted boxes to ground-truth boxes with IoU, then computing average precision (AP) over IoU thresholds. COCO keypoints keeps the whole AP machinery and swaps IoU for a pose similarity called **Object Keypoint Similarity (OKS)**, a number between 0 and 1.

A raw pixel distance cannot be the similarity on its own: 10 px is a big miss on a child far away and nothing on a person filling the frame, and a 10 px miss on an eye is worse than on a hip, because people themselves disagree more about where a hip is.

blocks.caption: d_i is the distance between predicted and ground-truth keypoint i, v_i is the ground-truth visibility flag, s is the object scale and kappa_i a per-keypoint falloff.

blocks.md:
Each term is a **keypoint similarity** between 0 and 1, an unnormalized Gaussian of the distance. The object scale $s$ is the square root of the person's segmentation area, which makes OKS scale invariant. The constants come from data: COCO had 5000 val images annotated more than once, measured each keypoint type's spread $\sigma_i$ relative to scale, and set $\kappa_i = 2\sigma_i$.

The published $\sigma$ values are .026 (nose), .025 (eyes), .035 (ears), .079 (shoulders), .072 (elbows), .062 (wrists), .107 (hips), .087 (knees) and .089 (ankles). Keypoints with $v = 0$ do not count, and the predicted visibility is ignored.

**Worked example.** One person, ground-truth segment area 9000 px squared, so $s = 94.87$. Five labeled keypoints, with prediction errors:

- nose: off by (4, 3), so $d = 5$, $\kappa = 0.052$, $s\kappa = 4.93$
- left shoulder: off by (6, 8), $d = 10$, $s\kappa = 14.99$
- left wrist: off by (-12, -9), $d = 15$, $s\kappa = 11.76$
- left hip: off by (-5, 6), $d = 7.81$, $s\kappa = 20.30$
- left knee: off by (8, -6), $d = 10$, $s\kappa = 16.51$

blocks.title: Per-keypoint similarity for the worked example

scenes.caption: Actual errors: similarities 0.598, 0.800, 0.444, 0.929, 0.832. The mean, OKS = 0.721. The wrist (15 px) costs the most, the nose loses 0.4 for only 5 px.
Same 5 px error on every keypoint: the nose scores 0.598 but the hip scores 0.970. Tight sigma means facial points must be nearly perfect.

blocks.caption: Same formula as pycocotools: vars = (2 sigma) squared, e = d squared / vars / area / 2, similarity = exp(-e).

blocks.prompt: With OKS = 0.721, at which of COCO's ten thresholds (0.50, 0.55, ..., 0.95) does this prediction count as a true positive?
blocks.reveal: At 0.50, 0.55, 0.60, 0.65 and 0.70: five of ten. It fails 0.75 and everything stricter. COCO's main AP averages over all ten thresholds, so this pose earns credit on half of them, and AP at OKS 0.75 (the strict metric) counts it as a miss.

scenes.caption: At the worked example's scale, the nose curve collapses within about 10 px while the hip stays above 0.9 out to 8 px.
The custom curve starts at the wrist sigma, 0.062, and passes the 15 px wrist point at 0.444.
Halve the person's scale to s = 47 (a person a quarter the area) and every curve tightens: the same pixel error now costs far more.

blocks.md: COCO's interpretation of $\kappa = 2\sigma$: an error of one, two or three human standard deviations gives similarity $e^{-1/8} = 0.88$, $e^{-4/8} = 0.61$ and $e^{-9/8} = 0.32$. The COCO page also reports that median human OKS is about 0.91, so a model at 0.95 is already inside annotator noise.

OKS is averaged per object over *labeled* keypoints, so a person with only 4 labeled points counts as much as one with 17. Also, persons too small to have keypoint labels are not evaluated, and at most 20 detections per image are scored. Comparing OKS numbers across datasets with different skeletons or sigmas is meaningless.

blocks.question: In the worked example the wrist's ground truth is changed to v = 0 (not labeled). What happens to OKS?
options: It stays 0.721, since prediction quality did not change
It drops, because a keypoint is now missing
It rises to 0.790, the mean of the other four similarities
It becomes undefined
blocks.explain: Unlabeled ground-truth keypoints are removed from both numerator and denominator. Dropping the worst term (0.444) leaves (0.598 + 0.800 + 0.929 + 0.832) / 4 = 0.790.

blocks.question: Two models both miss every keypoint by 6 px on the same people. Model A's errors are on the face; model B's are on hips and knees. Which has higher OKS?
options: Model A, faces are small so errors matter less
They are equal, since distances are equal
Model B, because hips and knees have larger sigma so the same distance is penalized less
It depends only on the person's area
blocks.explain: With the same d and s, the similarity depends on kappa. Hip and knee sigmas (.107, .087) are three to four times the face sigmas (.025 to .035), so B keeps much higher similarities.

lessons.title: Real-time tracking, 3D lifting and joint angles for apps

blocks.md:
Phone apps cannot afford a Faster R-CNN plus an HRNet per frame. **BlazePose** (Bazarevsky et al., 2020) is built for one person in real time on a phone: 33 keypoints at over 30 frames per second on a Pixel 2. Two ideas make it cheap.

First, a **detector-tracker** pipeline. A light detector runs only when needed. It finds the face, a fairly rigid part, and predicts alignment values: the midpoint of the hips, the radius of a circle around the whole body, and the body's tilt. On later frames the tracker reuses the previous frame's keypoints to place the crop. Second, heatmaps help training but are dropped from the deployed model. The network has a heatmap-and-offset head plus a coordinate regression head. Only regression runs on the phone.

scenes.caption: Frame 1: no previous pose, so the detector runs, then the tracker predicts keypoints inside the aligned crop.
Frames 2 to 4: the crop comes from the previous frame's keypoints, so only the tracker runs. This is where the frame rate comes from.
Frame 5: the tracker's person-presence output drops (the person stepped away), so on frame 6 the detector runs again.

blocks.md:
**MediaPipe Pose Landmarker** packages a BlazePose variant. Per the docs, it returns 33 `Landmarks` with x and y normalized to [0, 1] by image width and height, a relative depth z (origin at the hip midpoint), and a `visibility` likelihood. It also returns `WorldLandmarks`: x, y, z in meters with the hip midpoint as origin.

Getting 3D from one camera is ill-posed, yet Martinez et al. (2017) showed a strong baseline: "lift" 2D keypoints to 3D with a plain fully connected network (linear layers of 1024 units, batch norm, ReLU, dropout, residual connections). Given ground-truth 2D joints, it beat the best prior result on Human3.6M by about 30%, which suggested that much of 3D error comes from bad 2D detection.
Applications rarely use raw coordinates. They compute **joint angles**. The knee angle is the angle at the knee between the vector to the hip and the vector to the ankle:

blocks.caption: 180 degrees is a straight leg; smaller means more bent.

blocks.title: Knee angle from three image keypoints
blocks.code:
import math
hip, knee, ankle = (210, 300), (262, 385), (220, 468)
u = (hip[0] - knee[0], hip[1] - knee[1])
v = (ankle[0] - knee[0], ankle[1] - knee[1])
dot = u[0] * v[0] + u[1] * v[1]
cos_t = dot / (math.hypot(*u) * math.hypot(*v))
cos_t = max(-1.0, min(1.0, cos_t))  # guard rounding
theta = math.degrees(math.acos(cos_t))

scenes.caption: Image coordinates in pixels; y grows downward, which does not change the angle.
Vectors from the knee to each neighbor.
Lengths 99.64 and 93.02 give the cosine. Clamping avoids acos errors when rounding pushes a straight leg to -1.0000000002.
The knee is bent to about 122 degrees, a partial squat.

blocks.prompt: A camera faces a person squatting toward it. In world coordinates (meters) hip = (0.10, 0, 0), knee = (0.12, 0.20, -0.36), ankle = (0.11, 0.62, -0.30): the thigh points at the camera. What knee angle do the 3D points give, and what does the 2D image (drop z) give?
blocks.reveal: 3D: u = (-0.02, -0.20, 0.36), v = (-0.01, 0.42, 0.06), cosine -0.356, so about 111 degrees, a real squat. 2D: u = (-0.02, -0.20), v = (-0.01, 0.42), cosine -0.992, so about 173 degrees, a nearly straight leg. The thigh is foreshortened toward the camera. Simplified: this drops z (an orthographic view); a real camera adds perspective, but the effect is the same. Use 3D world landmarks or film from the side.

blocks.title: Counting squats from knee angles: one threshold versus hysteresis

scenes.caption: One real squat over 16 frames. Keypoint jitter makes the angle wobble around 130 on the way down and up.
One threshold at 130 (down below, up when back above) counts a rep at frames 4, 11 and 13: three reps for one squat.
Hysteresis: enter "down" only below 100 (frame 7), count a rep only when back above 160 (frame 14). Jitter between the thresholds does nothing: one rep.

blocks.md: Keypoints are noisy, especially when occluded. Before writing rules on them: check per-keypoint visibility or score, prefer 3D world landmarks or a side view for sagittal angles such as the knee, smooth over a few frames, and use two thresholds (hysteresis) rather than one.

blocks.question: A squat-depth checker flags every rep as too shallow, but only for users who film from directly in front. What is the most likely cause?
options: The OKS sigma for knees is too large
Foreshortening: in a frontal 2D view the thigh points at the camera, so the 2D knee angle looks straighter than it is
The heatmap resolution is too low
Hysteresis thresholds are too far apart
blocks.explain: A 2D angle measures the projection. When thigh or shin points toward the camera, it shrinks in the image and the projected angle opens up (111 degrees in 3D looked like 173 in the example). OKS sigmas only affect evaluation.

blocks.question: Why can BlazePose drop its heatmap branch at inference and still benefit from it?
options: The heatmap and offset losses supervise shared features during training, and the regression head uses those features at inference
Heatmaps were only used to visualize results
The heatmaps are cached from the first frame
MediaPipe computes heatmaps on the GPU separately
blocks.explain: The paper uses heatmap and offset losses only in training, then removes those output layers. They act as extra supervision that shapes the shared features, while the cheap regression head produces the coordinates at run time.
